verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of David, a psalm. YHWH, you have searched me, and you know.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, a song of David. LORD, you have searched me through — and you know me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open quietly, almost as an admission, not as a boast. The psalm begins with a title that was sung or read before the poem itself, and ends with a verb that is left without an object: "you know" — and the singer does not say what or whom. Let the pause after "you know" carry the weight; the rest of the psalm fills it in.

The verb chaqar is the language of mining and of judges: to dig, to probe, to examine a case until nothing is hidden (Prov 25:2 uses it for kings searching out a matter). Jeremiah 17:10 has God "searching the heart and testing the kidneys," and Radak ties our verse to exactly that. The KJV "searched me" is sound but sounds mild to an English ear; this is cross-examination, not a glance. The KJV also prints the title as a separate verse zero, which is a matter of numbering, not text. The Hebrew counts it as part of verse 1.

philological_notes.note: To search out, probe, examine thoroughly: the verb of mining, of judicial inquiry and of God testing the heart. Here the object is the speaker himself, not a matter or a case.

Traditionally 'to the choirmaster' or 'overseer' (KJV 'chief Musician'): a participle of the root that means to excel or to oversee, so a title for the one who directs the temple music. The exact duty is not certain.

verses.translation_literal: You, you know my sitting and my rising; you understand my thought from afar.
verses.translation_dramatic: You — you know when I sit down and when I stand up. You understand what I am thinking while it is still far off.
verses.directors_commentary:
The pronoun "you" stands alone at the head of the line, and the whole verse leans on it: not "the world," not "I myself," but you. Play it as a hush, not a shout.

"Sitting and rising" is a merism, two ends that mean everything between, and the daily round of an ancient household is behind it: sitting at the gate, rising at dawn. Radak says the pair shows the will behind each movement, since one first decides in the heart to rise. The KJV "thought" is right for re'i, which is not the usual word; the root is that of re'yon, "thought," known from Aramaic (Eccl 2:22, Ibn Ezra). The older translation also moves "afar off" onto the thought, which is correct: the Hebrew says that God understands the thought from a distance. Whether that distance is in space or in time is open: Radak and Meiri take it as time, "before I think it," and Metzudat David as "from the moment I was created." Rashi, taking re'i as "my friend," reads the verse as God drawing him from afar toward his friendship. The actors should take the thought, the reading most of the commentators share.

philological_notes.note: 'My thought', a rare noun from the root of re'yon 'thought' (Aramaic-influenced). It is not re'a 'friend', though Rashi takes it that way; most commentators agree on 'thought'. The lamed is the object marker here.
'From afar'; could be spatial or temporal ('from long before'), as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it.

verses.translation_literal: My going and my lying-down you have sifted, and all my ways you have been familiar with.
verses.translation_dramatic: My path and my resting place — you have gone round them both, and sifted them. There is no road of mine you have not walked beside until it is familiar.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 2 gave the two postures; verse 3 adds two more: walking and lying down. Together they are the four of daily life (Radak, Ibn Ezra, who connects them to the four actions of the Shema in Deut 6:7). Let the pace slow with "lying down": the one is a road, the other a bed, and God is at both.

The key verb zerita is a real fork. If it comes from zarah, it means to winnow, to throw grain in the wind so the husk blows off and the kernel is left; so the YLT's "fanned." If it comes from zer, the gold rim or wreath on the ark (Exod 25:24, as Rashi and Radak say), it means to surround. The KJV "compassest" takes the second. Both pictures say the same thing in different ways: nothing of me is out of God's sight, whether by sifting or by surrounding. The last verb hiskanta, "you have been familiar with," is the one of Num 22:30 (the donkey's "was I ever accustomed"), and Radak, Rashi and Metzudat Zion all say it means long habit. This is not distant knowledge, it is the knowing of an old companion.

philological_notes.note: Either 'you have winnowed, sifted' (from zarah) or 'you have encircled' (denominative from zer 'wreath, border'). Rashi and Radak take the second sense, citing zer zahav; Rashi also notes a rabbinic homily on winnowing (Niddah 31a).
'You have become familiar with', 'you have made [me] accustomed': the same root as in Num 22:30 'was I ever wont (hascen hiscanti)'. It expresses knowledge from habit, not mere data.
'My lying down', an Aramaic-flavoured form of the verb 'to crouch, lie' (Heb. ravatz); Radak points to the Targum's rav'ut. The Hebrew form is rare.

verses.translation_literal: For there is no word on my tongue — behold, YHWH, you know all of it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before the word has reached my tongue, before the breath has shaped it — there it is already in your hand, whole, every syllable of it known. The lips have not parted; you have heard the speech.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse begins with 'for', and it does a quiet job: it gives the reason for the verse before. Verse 3 said that God is familiar with all the psalmist's ways; here the same familiarity reaches into speech that has not been spoken. Most of the classical commentators (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Malbim) read it this way: the word is not yet finished on the tongue, and God already knows all of it. Radak gives that reading too, but prefers a second one: the speaker may plan a sentence in the heart, yet what actually comes out of the mouth is something only God foresees, and he points to Proverbs 16:1, 'the plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD'. An actor can play either: calm wonder at being known, or a small shiver at being known better than one knows oneself.

The KJV keeps 'For', but then adds a 'but' the Hebrew does not have: 'there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo...' That 'but' turns it into an 'except that' sentence, and it makes the line read as a concession. The Hebrew has no connecting word at all: a flat statement, then הֵן, 'behold', then the address. The sentences simply stand side by side, and the pause between them is the drama. BBE goes further and interprets it as 'which is not clear to you'. The final word כֻלָּהּ, 'all of it', is feminine, pointing back to מִלָּה, 'word', and it is the emphatic point: not a general sense of the word, but all of it.

philological_notes.note: 'Word, utterance'. It is a rare poetic word in Hebrew (the usual word for 'word' is דבר) and appears chiefly in Job and the Psalms. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'speech'.
'Behold, lo'. An interjection that points at something right in front of you. It marks the turn from the speaker's tongue to God's knowledge.

verses.translation_literal: Behind and before you have besieged me, and you have set upon me your palm.
verses.translation_dramatic: Behind me, before me — you have closed the ring. There is no gap in the wall, no road left open. And over me, laid down and weighing, the flat of your hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture here is of enclosure. The verb צַרְתָּנִי is the same as the one used for besieging a city, and most of the commentators take it so: Ibn Ezra reads it as 'you have laid siege to me' and sums up, 'there is no siege and no distress like this'; Metzudat David and Malbim spell it out, with God as the army that surrounds a little city so that nobody can get out. Malbim adds that the hand is on top of the psalmist too, so that he cannot rise above God's authority either. Radak, though, reports the reading of his father, Joseph Kimhi: the verb is the other צור, 'to form, to fashion', and the verse is about the shaping of the embryo in the mother's womb, with the hand set on it like a measure (he compares the cheese-pressing image of Job 10:10). The second reading anticipates verses 13–16, where the psalm does turn to the womb; on the first, the verse belongs with the story of being watched and held.

The KJV 'beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me' has the right siege sense, but 'beset' is archaic and it loses the force of a closed ring. 'Hand' is also not quite right: the Hebrew word כַּף is the palm, the flat of the hand, which is the part that presses and covers. 'Laid' is a soft rendering of וַתָּשֶׁת, which is 'to set, to place', as one sets down a weight. For the actor: the palm is not a caress. It rests, and the weight is felt. Rashi, in his Old French gloss, hears a restraint in it.

philological_notes.note: From צור 'to besiege, to confine' (the sense of Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Malbim) or, on the second reading, from צור 'to form, shape' (Radak's report of his father). The word allows both readings and the next verses make the second one possible.

'Your palm'. The suffix -ָכה for 'your' (masculine singular) is an older, fuller form of the ending, which Meiri points out and compares with יָרֵכָה in Exodus 13:15. The word is the palm, the hollow of the hand, not the whole hand (יד).

'Behind and before'. Ibn Ezra glosses קדם here as 'in front'. The same word also means 'east', which sets up verse 9 (the dawn, the sea); that is my reading, not a point any commentator in the packet makes.

verses.translation_literal: Too wonderful [is] knowledge for me; too high — I am not able [to reach] it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Such knowing is too wonderful for me. It stands too high; I cannot climb to it.
verses.directors_commentary:
A breath is released: the singer stops arguing and stands in awe, or in fear. It is a short, flat verse after the long chain before it, and it should be played with a short silence on each side.

The word pele' ("wonder") belongs to marvels that surpass human understanding; it is the angel's name in Judg 13:18, which the Metzudat Zion cites for the Ketiv. The consonants as written (the Ketiv) spell pil'iyah as pil'i plus a final he, "my wonder," and the reading (the Qere) smooths it to the adjective, as Meiri notes. "Knowledge" (da'at) is the noun of the verb used five times since verse 1. The KJV "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" is close. The KJV adds "such" and moves the verb "attain" out of the Hebrew, which has only "I am not able to it"; the verb is simply left out. Meiri and Metzudat David both hear a threat in the verse: this is the knowledge from which no hiding place can be found. Malbim separates two kinds of marvel: one that an individual cannot grasp, and one that no one could.

philological_notes.note: Reading (Qere) 'wonderful'; the written form (Ketiv) is pil'iyah spelled with final he after yod, which Meiri and Metzudat Zion link to pil'i 'wonder' (Judg 13:18).
'It is set on high', 'too high to reach': a word for fortified, unreachable heights. Metzudat Zion glosses it as strong.

verses.translation_literal: Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?
verses.translation_dramatic: Where can I go to be out of your spirit? Where can I run to be out of your sight?
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the psalm turns from knowing to place. These are rhetorical questions, not travel planning: "where" is asked twice, with the same rising tone, and the answer is already known to the audience. Don't deliver them as a real search; deliver them as a man who has already tried.

The two nouns say different things. ruach is "spirit" or "breath," God's active presence; panim is literally "face," what one stands before. The KJV's "presence" is a good rendering of panim, but loses the body image and the sense of being looked at. Radak calls the doubling a variation in words for the same thing. Metzudat Zion reads ruach as anger ("do not hurry in your spirit," Eccl 7:9), and Metzudat David follows that, as the Targum also does ("from before your anger"): fleeing from a wrathful God rather than from a God who is merely everywhere. Meiri's "your will and decree" is a third option. The speaker's verb barach, "flee," is that of Jonah running to Tarshish (Jonah 1:3), which a first audience would hear behind these words.

philological_notes.note: 'From your spirit': God's active, breathing presence; but Metzudat Zion, Metzudat David and the Targum understand it as anger and Meiri as will.
'I will flee': the verb for running away from something, as in Jonah 1:3 (own observation).

verses.translation_literal: If I ascend [to] the heavens, there [are] you; and [if] I spread [my bed in] Sheol — there, you!
verses.translation_dramatic: Let me climb to the heavens — you are there, waiting at the top of the stair. Let me make my bed down in Sheol, in the deep silence of the dead — and there too, you.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first of a series of impossible escapes, and the verse sets two extremes against each other: the heavens, as high as one can go, and Sheol, as deep as one can go. Together they mean everywhere. Ibn Ezra explains the second as the lowest part of the earth, the opposite of the heavens. The tone is not triumphant. This is a person who has been looking for a hiding place and finding there is none, and the actor should play the second line a notch quieter than the first, because Sheol is where the voice goes down.

The KJV has 'if I make my bed in hell', and that is its most famous mistake here: Sheol is not the hell of later Christian imagination but the underworld, the resting place of all the dead, good and bad (the packet's name-note says the same). The word choice also matters for the verb: וְאַצִּיעָה is a Hiphil, 'I spread out (a bed, a couch)', and Ibn Ezra notes that it is transitive, with the object ('my bed') left unsaid; Rashi and Metzudat Zion tie it to מַצָּע and מִשְׁכָּב, a mattress or a place to lie down. Radak takes this a step further: Sheol is the bed man is laid in at death. The picture is the same as verse 3's 'lying down', though the word is different. The Hebrew of the second half has no verb at all: just הִנֶּךָּ, 'there, you!', which is a gasp, not a statement. The KJV adds 'thou art there' twice and so removes the difference between the two clauses. Note also that the Hebrew has 'the heavens' in the plural, as it always does.

philological_notes.note: 'I ascend'. An Aramaic form of the verb (סלק, 'to go up') rather than the usual Hebrew עלה. Ibn Ezra says it is the same as the Targum's word, and Metzudat Zion compares Daniel 7. It lends the verse a faintly foreign, archaic sound.
'And I spread (a bed)'. Hiphil of יצע, with an unstated object ('my bed'); related to מַצָּע and יָצוּעַ, 'couch'. Radak says Sheol is called a bed because it is man's bed in death.
Sheol, the underworld, the place of the dead. Not 'hell': it holds everyone, and it is understood as beneath the earth, set against the heavens.

verses.translation_literal: [If] I lift [the] wings of dawn, [if] I dwell at [the] end of [the] sea,
verses.translation_dramatic: If I took up the wings of the dawn, and made my home at the far edge of the sea —
verses.directors_commentary:
From up and down to east and west. The dawn is the image: the light that runs across the sky from one horizon to the other in a moment, and the poet lends it wings. The verse does not finish its sentence. It is the "if" clause of a thought that verse 10 resolves, so keep the voice rising and unresolved at the end.

The "sea" for an Israelite is the Mediterranean, which lies to the west; Ibn Ezra notes that "sea" is the Hebrew word for west for this reason. "The end of the sea" is therefore the far western horizon, beyond which no Israelite sailed — the end of the known world. The KJV "uttermost parts of the sea" is a good rendering. The "wings of the morning" are a famous English phrase, and the KJV is faithful to the Hebrew; what the English misses is that "lifting" wings (esa kanfei) is the ordinary verb for taking something up, so the poet imagines picking up a pair of wings, and the dawn is the one that wears them. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David all read the wings as the speed of the dawn light spreading, not as the wings of a bird.

philological_notes.note: 'Wings of dawn': the dawn light seen as winged, spreading from east to west in an instant. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David all explain it by the speed of dawn.
'The end of the sea': the far west, the Mediterranean's farthest edge. Ibn Ezra notes yam can mean 'west' but here means sea itself.

verses.translation_literal: Even there your hand will lead me, and your right [hand] will grasp me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even there it is your hand that leads me, and your right hand that holds me fast.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sentence that verses 8 and 9 were holding back finally lands, and with it the tone of the whole psalm turns: the flight does not end in escape, it ends in a hand. Ibn Ezra puts it in one line: "I was fleeing from your hand into your hand." Play the line gently. It is a comfort and a trap at the same moment, and the singer has not decided which.

Two hands, with two verbs: yad leads (nachah, the word for guiding a flock or a blind man), and yamin, the right hand, "grasps" (achaz, to take firm hold). The right hand is the hand of strength and of oaths. The KJV's "hold me" is a bit soft for achaz, which also means to seize or take possession (it is used of land). "Lead" is accurate, but note that the tenses in the Hebrew are imperfect, so it can be read as "leads" or "will lead", as at present or as a future promise. Malbim sees the left hand guiding and the right hand holding back, which is his own picture, not the text's.

philological_notes.note: 'It will grasp, seize me': a firm grip, also used for taking possession of land. Stronger than 'hold'.
'It will lead me': the verb for guiding, as a shepherd leads. Metzudat Zion glosses it as conducting.

verses.translation_literal: And I said, "Surely darkness will crush me, and night [will be] light about me."
verses.translation_dramatic: And I thought: perhaps the dark will swallow me, and the night itself will be the light that hides me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last hiding place is the night. "And I said" means, as Ibn Ezra puts it, "I said in my heart": this is thinking, not speaking. In a world without street lights, the dark is real cover: thieves, adulterers and murderers wait for it (Job 24:13-17), and the speaker reaches for it as a child pulls a blanket over his head.

The verb yeshufeni is the knot. It is used of the serpent and the heel (Gen 3:15), where it means to crush or bruise, and Job 9:17 uses it of a storm. Rashi, Radak and Meiri take it from nashaf ("twilight"), so to darken, to cover, and the KJV ("cover me") follows. The YLT's "bruiseth" follows the other root. So "crush" or "cover" are both possible; "crush" is what the Hebrew word usually means, and the darkness would then be a force that falls on him. The second clause is also awkward: "night — light about me." Rashi takes it as "night will be dark about me" (or means darkness, as in Job 37:11); the KJV and YLT read it as "night is light." Both fit verse 12, and I kept the plain order with the contradiction visible.

philological_notes.note: Either 'it will crush, bruise me' (as in Gen 3:15) or 'it will cover me in darkness' (from nashaf 'twilight'). Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all take the covering sense; Ibn Ezra treats them as two roots with one meaning.
'Light about me' (or 'light for me, behind me'). Rashi reads 'or here as darkness, ofel, comparing Job 37:11; most others read it as light.

verses.translation_literal: Even darkness does not darken from you, and night like day lights up; like darkness, like light.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the dark does not darken anything from you. The night burns bright as noon; and the black, and the blaze — to you they are one and the same.
verses.directors_commentary:
The previous verse ended with the psalmist's hope that darkness might cover him, and this verse answers it: it cannot. The line is built on sound. The root חשך, 'to be dark', appears three times (חֹשֶׁךְ, יַחְשִׁיךְ, כַּחֲשֵׁיכָה), and the root אור, 'light', answers it twice (יָאִיר, כָּאוֹרָה). An English reader gets this only if a word is repeated: 'darkness does not darken', not 'darkness hideth not'.

The verb יַחְשִׁיךְ is a Hiphil, 'to make dark', and the classical commentators read it as transitive with an unstated object. Ibn Ezra says it plainly: 'darkness does not darken anything from you'; Radak says the same ('it does not darken anything from you so that you do not see it'); Metzudat David has it too. The other way to read it is intransitive, 'is not dark to you', which is the sense in BBE ('the dark is not dark to you'). The KJV's 'hideth not from thee' is a paraphrase that trades the verb for another, and it adds a 'but' before 'the night' that the Hebrew, with its plain 'and', does not have. The last phrase is the terse, almost blunt כַּחֲשֵׁיכָה כָּאוֹרָה, 'as darkness, as light', with no verb and no 'to thee'; the KJV expands it to 'the darkness and the light are both alike to thee'. Ibn Ezra compares the shorthand to 'like servant, like master', and Radak to 'for you are like Pharaoh': two things set side by side, each like the other. Play it as a closing click, not a lecture.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of חשך, 'to make dark'. STEPBible glosses it 'is [too] dark', which reads it as intransitive; Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as transitive with an unstated object ('darkness darkens nothing from you'). The intransitive 'is not dark to you' is the alternative.

'As darkness, as light'. A compressed double comparison with nothing to carry it. Ibn Ezra compares it with 'like servant, like master' (the two stand on a par), and Radak with 'for you are like Pharaoh'. The two nouns rhyme in sound (-ah, -ah).

verses.translation_literal: For you, you acquired my kidneys; you screened me in the belly of my mother.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it was you. You took hold of the deep places in me, the hidden seat of every thought, and made them yours. You drew the dark around me like a curtain, there in my mother's body, where no eye had ever been.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker pivots from "you cannot be escaped" to "you made me", and the argument is a legal one: whatever God owns, God cannot be kept out of. The verb קנה means "acquire", and it is the verb of ownership and of creation both ("maker [qoneh] of heaven and earth", Gen 14:19). The KJV's "possessed" keeps the first sense and loses the second; the ASV's "form" does the reverse. Say it with both: God made them, and they are God's.

The "kidneys" (כליות) are not an organ-list entry. In Hebrew psychology the kidneys are the interior seat of conscience, desire and counsel (Ps 7:10, 16:7, Jer 11:20: God "tests kidneys and heart"). The KJV's "reins" is an archaism that hides the plain word; modern readers hear a medical joke where the ancient audience heard "my innermost self". Radak and Metzudat Zion say exactly that: the kidneys are what counsel a person. The second verb, תסכני, is a rare word: "you screened/covered me" (Rashi equates it with סוכך), picking up the darkness of verses 11-12; some modern lexica hear "you wove me", which fits the textile image of verse 15. The womb is the dark that is no dark to God.

philological_notes.note: Acquire, buy, and by extension create. Ownership and making are one act here: what God made, God owns, and therefore knows.
Kidneys: the hidden inner seat of thought and conscience, not a mere organ. The KJV 'reins' is an archaic rendering.
Cover, screen, shield; Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as תסוככני. A weaving sense ('you knitted me') is argued by some modern lexica from a different root, but it is uncertain.

verses.translation_literal: I will thank you for [this]: that I am set apart in awesome [ways]; wonderful are your works, and my self knows [it] exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will give thanks to you, for I am made of wonders that make me tremble. Wonderful, wonderful are your works; and I know it, deep in myself, I know it well.
verses.directors_commentary:
The famous "fearfully and wonderfully made" is two verbs, not an adverb pair, and the KJV smooths a stranger sentence. נוראות is "awesome things", things that inspire fear, and נפליתי is a passive of the root פלא, "to be set apart, made distinct, marvellous": "I have been set apart [by] awesome acts" (so YLT: "with wonders I have been distinguished"; Radak: "awesome acts are in my forming"). The psalmist is not praising his own looks; he is shaking at how his body was done. The rhyme of נפליתי and נפלאים is deliberate: the same root sounds twice, so the speaker is marvellous and the works that did it are marvellous.

The last clause, "my nefesh knows very well", is the point of the speech: this is knowledge from the inside, the self recognising its Maker's craft. The KJV adds "and that", turning the clause into a subordinate; the Hebrew simply says it flatly. Ibn Ezra notes that מאד can attach either to the knowing or to "wonderful", and both are possible.

philological_notes.note: Niphal 'I have been set apart / made wonderfully distinct', from the same root as נִפְלָאִים 'wonderful' in the next clause: a deliberate sound-and-sense echo.
'Awesome things', from the root of fear; Ibn Ezra takes it as an adjective of the acts (cf. Ex 34:10).

token_glosses.gloss: I am set apart / made wonderful

verses.translation_literal: My bones were not hidden from you, when I was made in the secret place, woven in the lowest parts of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Not even my bones were hidden from you, when I was being made in secret, in the dark below, stitched together in the lowest places of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two images carry the verse. First, עצמי: "my bones" (the Masoretic vowel is that of "my frame, my very self"; Radak and Metzudat Zion discuss both). The KJV's "substance" is a safe abstraction; the Hebrew is concrete, a skeleton being built out of sight. Second, רקמתי, "I was embroidered": the word is used of multi-coloured needlework (Ex 26:36, Ps 45:15), and it describes the body as fine, patterned fabric. The KJV's "curiously wrought" is a nice Elizabethan phrase that modern ears hear wrongly ("curious" meant "with care").

The "lowest parts of the earth" is a metaphor for the womb, a dark, enclosed place, and also an echo of the creation of Adam from the soil (Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Moses on this). "Made in secret" (עשיתי) is a shorter, rougher word than the fine embroidery of the next verb; Radak links it to a physical sense of pressing, as in making cheese. Keep the contrast: rough hands, then fine needlework.

philological_notes.note: 'Embroidered, woven in many colours'; used for fine textile work, so the body is imagined as a patterned cloth.
'In the lower parts of the earth': a figure for the womb, dark and low, echoing Adam's creation from the ground.

verses.translation_literal: My unformed mass your eyes saw, and on your scroll all of them were written, days [that] were formed, and to it [Ketiv: not] one among them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before I had a shape, your eyes were on me, a shapeless thing, and in your book every one of them was already written: the days that would be formed for me, when not one of them yet was.
verses.directors_commentary:
גלמי, "my unformed mass", occurs only here in the Bible. It names the embryo before it has features: later Hebrew uses the same root for a half-finished piece of woodwork or an unshaped lump. The KJV's "substance yet being unperfect" is clear enough; "unformed" is closer. God's eyes see the lump, and the Hebrew keeps the sound of the heavy, blunt word on purpose.

Then comes the sentence the KJV rewrites. "All of them were written": in the Hebrew the pronoun "them" has no antecedent in the verse, so the commentators supply one (the limbs: Ibn Ezra, Radak; the days: most modern readers), and "days were formed, and one of them was his" (the Qere) makes the days the thing God drew up in advance. The Ketiv reads "and not one of them", "before any of them existed", which is what the KJV's "when as yet there was none of them" follows. The KJV also inserts "my members", which is not in the Hebrew at all. The scroll image is that of a royal scribe's register or a heavenly book of destiny (cf. Ps 56:8, Ex 32:32).

philological_notes.note: Hapax: 'my formless lump, my embryo before it had features'. Related to later גולם 'an unfinished vessel'.
Qere 'and to it (him) [belongs] one of them'; Ketiv 'and not one of them'. The two readings give opposite shapes to the end of the verse.

verses.translation_literal: And to me, how precious are your thoughts, O God! How vast are their sums!
verses.translation_dramatic: And to me, how precious they are, your thoughts, O God! How vast, how beyond all measure, their sum!
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes from awe at the body to awe at the mind behind it. The Hebrew is exclamation, not statement: "how!" opens both clauses. יקרו is "precious" and also "rare, hard to reach" (as in 1 Sam 3:1, "the word of the LORD was rare"): Radak and Meiri read it as "too precious for me to grasp". The KJV's "also" is a small invention that reads as the speaker adding a second thought; the Hebrew's opening "and to me" sets the speaker against God's own knowledge, which he has just said cannot be grasped.

The unusual noun רעיך is "your thoughts" (from רעיון), not "your friends" (רֵעַ) as the Targum and Rashi take it. The second clause plays on ראש: "head" and so "sum, total" (as in the census idiom "lift up the head", Ex 30:12), and עצם, "to be mighty" and so "to be many" (Jer 15:8). The images of counting prepare for the sand in the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Your thoughts' (רעיון); commentators also hear 'your friends' (the righteous), which Rashi and the Targum choose.
'Are mighty' and so 'are numerous'; see the same sense in Jer 15:8.
'Their heads', so 'their sums, their totals', as in the census idiom 'lift up the head' (Ex 30:12).

verses.translation_literal: I count them, more than sand they multiply; I awoke, and still I [am] with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: I would count them, and the count would drown. More than the sand they rise, grain upon grain upon grain, past all reckoning. And then I wake, the night lifting from me, and you are there. Still I am with you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the first half as a man who starts a task and watches it dissolve. 'Sand' (חוֹל) is the ancient Near East's stock image for the uncountable: it is what God promises Abraham's offspring in Genesis 22:17 and 32:12. The same verb (סָפַר, 'to count') also means 'to recount, to tell', so counting God's thoughts is also telling them, and in both senses the task cannot be done. The KJV's 'If I should count them' supplies a conditional the Hebrew does not state: the psalmist simply begins to count (אֶסְפְּרֵם), and the sand answers. It also writes 'they are more in number', which smooths the verb יִרְבּוּן, 'they multiply, they grow', a word of ongoing increase: the thoughts keep outrunning him.

The second half is the hinge of the verse, and the old readers split on it. Ibn Ezra and Radak take הֱקִיצֹתִי as waking from sleep: Ibn Ezra, that on waking there is no trace of sleep and he is still with God (and, in a second reading, that this is no ordinary dream); Radak, that the psalmist is so full of these thoughts that he dreams them in his sleep and, on waking, finds himself still with God in them. Meiri and Metzudat David hear something else: even if he gave up sleep and spent every day and night on the task, he still could not reach the end. Rashi turns it to the generations. The KJV's 'when I awake, I am still with thee' fixes the first reading and loses the open question. An actor can play either: a wake-up, or the exhausted end of a sleepless attempt. Either way the final word is עִמָּךְ, 'with you', and it closes the thought on presence, not on arithmetic. The scene turns from the vastness of God's thoughts to the nearness of God.

philological_notes.note: 'More than sand': the prefix מִן marks the comparison. Sand is the biblical image for what cannot be counted (Gen 22:17; 32:12), and here it is turned on its head: God's thoughts outnumber what is already uncountable.

Hiphil perfect, 'I awoke, I woke up'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as waking from sleep; Meiri and Metzudat David read it as a count carried on by day and night without sleep that still fails. The same form is a perfect, 'I have awoken', not a conditional 'when I awake' as in the KJV.

verses.translation_literal: If you would kill, O Eloah, the wicked, and men of bloods, turn away from me!
verses.translation_dramatic: If only you would strike the wicked down, O God! And you, men of blood, get away from me!
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here, abruptly, from wonder to violence, and the audience should feel the jolt. The Hebrew is "if you would kill, O Eloah, the wicked": a conditional that never finishes its main clause, or a wish (the BBE's "If only"; Rashi's "Would that you slay"). The KJV's "Surely thou wilt slay" turns a hope into a confident prediction and "ye bloody men" is a euphemism: אנשי דמים is "men of bloods", people who shed blood. Radak links the verse back to the last: the wicked keep the poet from his meditations on God.

The address changes in the middle: God, then the wicked directly ("turn away from me!"). The word אלוה is a rare, archaic singular of "God", and it makes the cry sound older and harsher.

philological_notes.note: Poetic singular of אלהים, used mostly in Job and in archaic verse.
'Men of bloods', plural 'bloods' meaning bloodshed or blood-guilt: killers.

verses.translation_literal: Who speak you for scheming, they lift up for emptiness, your foes.
verses.translation_dramatic: They say your name, but only to dress a plot. They raise it high, and it holds nothing: a great banner over an empty tent. These are your enemies, and they say your name as if it were theirs.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest verse of the stretch, and an actor should know that the Hebrew is knotted in three places. First, יֹאמְרֻךָ is 'they say you', with no preposition to tell us whether 'of you' or 'to you' is meant. Radak takes it as a spelling of ימרוך with the aleph dropped, and so 'they speak of you', as in 2 Sam 19:14, with the sense that they talk of God in the service of their own plans. Meiri finds it hard that 'saying' should take a direct object without ל, and so reads it from the root of Deut 26:17, 'you have declared (exalted) the LORD', as do Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion: the enemies 'exalt you'. In that reading they praise God for the sake of a scheme, saying 'the LORD is high, he does not stoop to watch the low world', and the praise is a cover for wrongdoing; Metzudat Zion adds that a yod stands for the aleph (cf. Isa 61:6). Second, נָשֻׂא is a final-aleph form of 'they lift up' (Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare Josh 10:24 and Ezek 39:26), so the line is a hollow lifting. Third, עָרֶיךָ is a rare word for 'adversaries', related to the ער of 1 Sam 28:16, and the object of the lifting is missing: the KJV and ASV supply 'thy name', which the Hebrew does not have, and which brings in the third commandment (Exod 20:7), a link some medievals make themselves. The KJV's 'speak against thee' is a harmonization: nothing says 'against'. The sense that survives every reading is a pious show that serves a scheme, which is why the speaker answers it in v. 21 with hatred of God's haters. The word מְזִמָּה is 'plan, scheme', often with a bad sense, and Metzudat Zion links it to זִמָּה, 'wickedness', in Lev 20:14.

philological_notes.note: Two ways of reading it. 'They speak of you': Radak (ימרוך with the aleph dropped, compared with 2 Sam 19:14). 'They exalt you': Meiri, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion, from the root of Deut 26:17 הֶאֱמַרְתָּ. Meiri objects that 'saying' needs ל before its object; Metzudat Zion notes the yod standing for aleph, as in Isa 61:6.
A final-aleph form that stands for a plural perfect, 'they lifted up' (Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare Josh 10:24 and Ezek 39:26). The verse leaves the object out; the KJV supplies 'thy name'.
'Your adversaries'. A rare word, glossed by Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion as 'your enemies'. Metzudat Zion compares 1 Sam 28:16.

verses.translation_literal: Is it not those who hate you, YHWH, I hate, and with those who rise up against you I quarrel?
verses.translation_dramatic: Those who hate you, LORD — shall I not hate them? Those who rise against you — shall I not stand against them, face to face, and quarrel?
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker comes out of the plain statement of v. 19 into a question that expects yes: 'Do I not hate...?' The speaker is not telling God about a private feeling. He is declaring loyalty and distancing himself from the people who spoke God's name for a scheme in v. 20; Meiri says he states this so that no one will mistake him for one of them. The verb at the end, אֶתְקוֹטָט, is a rare one: Ibn Ezra ties it to קוּט, 'to loathe' (Ps 95:10), and says the two halves of the line say the same thing twice; Radak and Meiri read it as 'quarrel' (קטטה), the language of the rabbis. The KJV's 'grieved' softens both: the verb is closer to 'loathe' or 'quarrel' than to sorrow, and מְשַׂנְאֶיךָ is plain 'those who hate you'. The Hebrew is blunt about hatred, and the English translators often put it behind 'grief' and 'those that rise up' for a modern ear. Malbim adds an interpretive point: hating the enemies of the one you love is the sign of love.

philological_notes.note: ב + תְּקוֹמֵם (H8618), 'one who rises up', with the suffix 'your': 'and with those who rise up against you'. Meiri equates it with במתקוממיך. Radak glosses it as 'those who hate you', comparing וּמִתְקוֹמְמִים בִּימִינֶךָ (Ps 17:7); Ibn Ezra simply labels it a descriptive term (תאר).
A rare verb, related either to קוּט, 'to loathe' (Ibn Ezra, comparing אָקוּט in Ps 95:10) or to קטטה, 'quarrel' (Radak and Meiri). The two readings are 'I loathe' and 'I contend'.

token_glosses.gloss: and with those who rise up against you

verses.translation_literal: With completeness of hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I hate them with a hatred that has no end to it, a hatred whole and entire. They have become my enemies too.
verses.directors_commentary:
תכלית שנאה is "the utmost of hatred", with the sense of an end-point reached: hatred with nothing left over (Metzudat David: "the end of hatred, beyond which there is none"). The KJV's "perfect hatred" is accurate in its old sense ("perfect" = complete) but a modern hearer takes it as an admirable or refined hatred. The verb and noun share a root: "hatred I hate", a cognate accusative that doubles the force, and the English keeps it.

The second half says what the hatred amounts to: the enemies of God have become the speaker's enemies. The Hebrew "they have become enemies to me" is a statement of adopted allegiance, which is how the ancient Near East understood loyalty in treaty language (to love the king's friends and hate his enemies). Meiri hears even this as a rejection of their company rather than a call to violence.

philological_notes.note: 'Completeness of hatred I hate them': a cognate figure; תכלית is 'end-point, completion'.

verses.translation_literal: Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me, and know my anxious thoughts.
verses.translation_dramatic: Search me, God, and know my heart. Test me, and know what goes round and round in me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone drops from the hot, loud denunciation to a quiet prayer: after judging others the speaker invites God to judge him. The two imperatives are matched pairs: "search" (חקר, to dig and probe, as for ore or a hidden matter) and "test" (בחן, to assay metal, Metzudat Zion: "as the smelter tests silver"), each followed by "and know". The KJV's "try me" is archaic. The second "know" repeats the first in the Hebrew, which the English keeps.

שרעפי is a rare word, "my disquieting thoughts", which Radak links to the "branches" of a tree (the thoughts that spread from the heart as branches do from the trunk). The KJV flattens it to "thoughts", losing both the anxiety and the branching image; the BBE's "wandering thoughts" is nearer. The same word is used in Ps 94:19 ("in the multitude of my cares within me").

philological_notes.note: Rare noun for anxious, branching thoughts; compare Ps 94:19. Radak links it to סעיף 'branch'.
'Test me', the verb of assaying metal; the speaker offers to be proved genuine.

verses.translation_literal: And see if a way of hurt is in me, and lead me in the way of old.
verses.translation_dramatic: And see whether there is any road of grief in me. And if there is, lead me out of it, and on to the road that was laid down long ago.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer closes on two roads. The KJV's "wicked way" is a moral gloss; עֹצֶב is "hurt, pain, grief" (as in Is 63:10, "they rebelled and grieved his holy spirit"), so the medieval commentators read "a way of rebellion" (Rashi, Radak, Meiri) or "a way that hurts God" (Metzudat David). STEPBible's "idol" is a different noun, עצב, also a word for idols (Ps 16:4), and Malbim hears the double: "a way of rebellion or idolatry". The sense is: is there anything in me that grieves you?

דרך עולם is "the way of old / everlasting". The KJV's "everlasting" is right as far as it goes. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri hear a second sense, the way of death ("the way of all the earth", 1 Kgs 2:2; "to his everlasting house", Eccl 12:5), so that the prayer is either "lead me in the good old way" or "take me from the world if I am wicked". The verse ends the psalm with that open question; the ending should not feel resolved.

philological_notes.note: 'A way of hurt/grief': the commentators read 'rebellion' via Is 63:10; the 'idol' reading (a different noun with the same consonants) is also proposed.
'The way of antiquity/eternity'; some read 'the way of death' (בית עולם, Eccl 12:5).
